question: How do pandas and built-in Python handle missing data, duplicates, value transformation, binning, outliers, sampling, dummy variables and string cleaning?

limits: Examples use the 2nd-edition API: fillna(method='ffill'), (np.abs(data) > 3).any(1), pd.value_counts, from numpy import nan as NA; several are deprecated or removed in current pandas (inferred from my knowledge of later pandas, not from the text).
Chapter says coverage is not comprehensive and regex writing is out of scope.
Says missing-data representation in pandas is 'somewhat imperfect' and under ongoing work.
The slow loop for multi-genre indicator variables is flagged as unsuitable for much larger data.
Outlier example uses random data without a seed; the 80% figure has no citation.
practices: Use dropna(how='all') or thresh=n to control how much missing data a row may hold before it is dropped (p.193-194).
Prefer fillna over dropping when dropping would discard other data in the row; use a dict for per-column fill values, or ffill with limit (p.195-196).
Analyse the missing data itself to find collection problems or bias before filling or dropping (p.192).
Use replace to turn sentinel values such as -999 into NaN, passing a list or dict for several values (p.200-201).
Lowercase before mapping with a dict, or pass a function to map, for element-wise recoding (p.199-200).
Use rename rather than copying a DataFrame to relabel axes (p.202).
Use cut for explicit bin edges and qcut for roughly equal-size bins from sample quantiles (p.203-205).
Use sample(n, replace=True) for random subsets and permutation plus take/iloc for shuffling (p.207).
Use get_dummies for categorical columns; combine with cut for binned indicators; for multi-membership columns, avoid the Python loop on large data and write to a NumPy array (p.208-211).
Use the Series .str methods instead of map for strings, because they skip NA values (p.217).
Compile a regex with re.compile when applying it to many strings, and use raw string literals (p.214).
Use 'x in s' to test for a substring; find returns -1 where index raises ValueError (p.212).
